items.value: The great evil of our age is overstrain (excessive labour)
items.reasoning: The passage's premise is stated in its second sentence: "An excessive amount of labour is rule today in every circle of society" — and everything after it is a consequence of that overstrain (the spiritual element cannot thrive, leisure cannot be used seriously, thinking is avoided, culture sinks to cinema and crime stories). B names that premise. D names only one of the listed consequences, so it is a detail rather than the idea the passage rests on; C is likewise a single sentence lifted out; A is a prescription the passage never makes.

items.value: Because he loves amusement and wants to be mentally idle
items.reasoning: The passage answers this directly: "He seeks not self-improvement, but entertainment which would enable him to be mentally idle and to forget his usual activities." That is exactly option D. B (no time) is contradicted by the passage, which says he has "little leisure" but chooses to fill it with entertainment; A is refuted by "or he cannot even if he wants to" being offered as an alternative rather than the reason; C introduces materialism, a word the passage never uses.

items.value: Only statement 2 — the ratio of very old and very young will decrease for a while
items.reasoning: Statement 2 is the passage's own definition: the dividend "is basically a swelling in the working age population, which conversely means that the relative ratio of very young and very old will, for a while, be on the decline" — so it happens by construction, i.e. invariably. Statement 1 fails because the passage makes education a condition for reaping the benefits, never an automatic consequence of the dividend. Statement 3 fails because the passage says nothing about the population growth rate stabilising, let alone quickly.

items.value: Neither inference is valid
items.reasoning: Inference 1 fails on the word "essential": the passage calls the dividend "a great window of opportunity" that "can be a source of energy and an engine of economic growth" — an opportunity, not a necessary condition, and many countries have grown fast without one. Inference 2 fails twice over: the passage speaks of "education, acquisition of skills and human capital" for reaping the dividend's benefits, not of *higher* education specifically, and not as an essential condition for rapid economic growth in general. An inference must follow from the passage as written, and both of these overstate it.

From (2) and (3): P + (P - 5) = 21, so P = 13 and Q = 8. From (5): X = P - 5 = 8. From (1): Z = X + 8 = 16. From (4): Y = 28 - X = 20. The total is 13 + 8 + 8 + 20 + 16 = 65 notebooks, and 65 x 40 = 2600. All five given conditions check out on these values.

items.value: The village clock is 5 minutes fast
items.reasoning: By the home clock the whole trip took 14:30 to 16:00, i.e. 90 minutes, of which 25 were spent at the village, leaving 65 minutes of driving. The return route is 1.25 times as long at twice the speed, so it takes 1.25/2 = 0.625 of the outward time; hence t + 0.625t = 65, giving t = 40 minutes out and 25 minutes back. So he reached the village at 15:10 by the home clock while the village clock read 15:15 — the village clock is 5 minutes fast.

items.value: 294 pens
items.reasoning: Writing A for the number A receives, the conditions give B = A/2, C = A/3, D = A/4, E = A/5, F = A/6. Every one of these, and A itself, must be even, so A must be divisible by 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12; the least such A is their LCM, 120. Then the shares are 120, 60, 40, 30, 24, 20 — all even — and their total is 294. Option A (147) is the answer to the same question without the even requirement, so it is the trap here.

items.value: Even both statements together cannot fix who sits on A's immediate left
items.reasoning: Statement-1 pairs B with C and D with E, which forces A and F to be the third opposite pair but fixes nothing about A's neighbours, so it is insufficient alone; Statement-2 places F beside B and says nothing about A at all, so it too is insufficient alone. Taken together: put B at a seat, F on its immediate left, then C sits opposite B and A opposite F, leaving D and E to fill the last two seats in either order — and one of those two seats is exactly the one on A's immediate left. So the neighbour is D or E and cannot be decided; the answer is that both statements together are not sufficient.

items.value: Both statements together are sufficient (Manisha is 31)
items.reasoning: Statement-1 alone gives only the difference of the two ages, and Statement-2 alone gives only their future ratio; each leaves one equation in two unknowns, so neither is enough by itself. Together, with M the mother's age, Manisha is M - 24 and 5(M - 24 + 5) = 3(M + 5), giving M = 55 and Manisha 31 — and the check works, since in 5 years they are 36 and 60, which is 3 : 5. So both together are sufficient.

items.value: Even both statements together cannot fix the third-period lecture
items.reasoning: Six one-hour lectures between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. fill six periods. Statement-1 only fixes the order A, F, C, which can sit in several places, and Statement-2 only puts B in the sixth period; neither alone names the third-period lecture. Together, the A-F-C block can occupy periods 1-3, 2-4 or 3-5 (with D and E in the leftover slots), making the third period C, F or A respectively — still undecided. Hence both statements together are not sufficient.

items.value: Only an educated population can best make use of the benefits of economic progress
items.reasoning: The passage's chain is that machine productivity yields leisure, that leisure "is apt to be tedious except to those who have intelligent activities and interests", and that "if a leisured population is to be happy, it must be an educated population" — i.e. education is what converts the fruits of economic progress into a good life, which is option A. C inverts this into a general claim that education raises happiness, dropping the leisure condition the passage insists on; B and D are prescriptions about what development or machinery *should* aim at, which the passage never makes.

items.value: There can be more than one reason why adults feel less thrilled by presents
items.reasoning: The opening sentence offers two candidate explanations joined by "or": "perhaps it is because we have too much already; or perhaps it is because we have lost the fullness of the joy of giving". Offering two possible reasons is precisely statement B. A is far too absolute — the passage says less thrill, not none; C is wrong because the author does offer reasons, however tentatively; D reads "capacity to feel the joy of loving or being loved" into a passage that speaks of giving and receiving presents.

items.value: The author is against worrying too much about the past and the future
items.reasoning: The author praises children because "they do not look too forward nor too far backward" and then turns the criticism on adults: "Perhaps we are too cautious, too anxious, too sceptical. Perhaps some of our cares would shrink if we thought less about them." That is opposition to excessive worry about what is behind and ahead, which is option A. D describes a loss the author regrets rather than a habit he argues against, and B and C misread the passage — he is not against thinking about gifts, nor is the loss of thrill itself the target of his complaint.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct
items.reasoning: Six numbers can be formed from three distinct digits, and each digit appears twice in each place, so x = 222(A + B + C). Since the digits are distinct and non-zero, the smallest possible sum is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, giving the smallest x as 222 x 6 = 1332, which is indeed the least 4-digit value — statement 1 is correct. For x to be a 3-digit number we would need A + B + C at most 4, which is impossible for three distinct non-zero digits, so x can never be a 3-digit number at all; the 888 in statement 2 is 222 x 4 and is unattainable, making statement 2 wrong.

items.value: 10 attempts
items.reasoning: The number of attempts needed for certainty is simply the number of PINs the rules allow. Writing the PIN as a > b > c drawn from 1 to 7 with a - b at least 2 and b - c at least 2, enumeration gives 6 choices with c = 1 (b = 3, 4, 5), 3 with c = 2 (b = 4, 5), and 1 with c = 3 (b = 5, a = 7) — a total of 10. This matches the standard count for choosing 3 of 7 with gaps of at least 2, which is C(5,3) = 10.

items.value: 24 triangles
items.reasoning: Eight equidistant points on a circle form 4 diameters, since each diameter joins a point to the one diametrically opposite and 8/2 = 4. Fixing a diameter as one side, the third vertex may be any of the remaining 6 points, and by the angle-in-a-semicircle theorem every such triangle is right-angled. That gives 4 x 6 = 24 triangles, with no double counting because each triangle contains exactly one diameter.

items.value: The data are inadequate — nothing is given about how a man's efficiency compares with a woman's
items.reasoning: Swapping the counts turns 24 men + 12 women into 12 men + 24 women, and which group is faster depends entirely on the unknown ratio of a man's daily work to a woman's. If they are equally efficient the answer is exactly 30 days; if a man works faster it is more than 30; if a woman works faster it is less than 30. Because all three outcomes remain possible, no conclusion can be drawn — and C is wrong precisely because it rules out the equal-efficiency case of exactly 30 days.

items.value: Remainder 0
items.reasoning: Factorise the divisor: 1261 = 13 x 97, and these are distinct primes. The product 91 x 92 x ... x 99 contains 91 = 7 x 13, so it is divisible by 13, and it also contains the factor 97 itself. Being divisible by both coprime factors, it is divisible by their product 1261, so the remainder is 0.

items.value: Both statements are correct
items.reasoning: For statement 1, cut two 8 cm x 8 cm squares off the 20 cm length, leaving a 4 cm x 8 cm strip that splits into two 4 cm x 4 cm squares — four squares in all, with areas 64 + 64 + 16 + 16 = 160, exactly the sheet's area. For statement 2, divide the sheet into five 4 cm x 8 cm rectangles and cut each along a diagonal, giving 10 triangles of area 16 sq cm each. Note that statement 1 does not require the squares to be equal, which is what makes it possible.

items.value: z < x < y
items.reasoning: The first condition gives 0.7x + y = 1.65y, so 0.7x = 0.65y and x = (13/14)y, which makes x smaller than y. The second gives 0.6x + z = 1.65z, so 0.6x = 0.65z and z = (12/13)x, which makes z smaller than x. Chaining them, z < x < y — for instance y = 14, x = 13, z = 12 satisfies both original statements exactly.
